Setting up of Airport Development Centre  
*301. SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering undertaking upgradation and 
modernization of airports in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether there is any plan to set up an Airport Development Centre for this 
purpose; and 
(d)if so, the details-thereof? 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The airp orts upgradation and 
modernization is an ongoing process. Such works are  taken up on operational 
requirements and demand from airlines. The importan t airport taken up for 
development are as under:— 
METRO AIRPORTS 
Delhi & Mumbai:—They have been restructured through Joint Venture route 
and are being modernized/upgraded. 
Kolkata:—Airports Authority of India (AAI) has been  mandated to take up 
upgradation/modernization of this airport and would be starting the work very 
shortly. 
Chennai:—Expansion/modernization of the airport is being discussed with the 
stakeholders as to availability of land for expansi on. A final decision in this 
regard would be taken up very soon. 
NON-METRO AIRPORTS:—AAI has been mandated to take u p the 
development of 35 Non-Metro Airports which are:— 
Ahmedabad, Amritsar, Guwahati, Jaipur, Udaipur, Trivandrum, Lucknow, Goa, 
Madurai, Mangalore, Agatti, Aurangabad, Khajuraho, Rajkot, Vadodara, 
Bhopal, Indore, Nagpur, Vishakapatnam, Trichy, Bhub aneshwar, Combatore, 
Patna, Port Blair, Varanasi, Agartala, Dehradun, Im phal, Ranchi, Raipur, 
Agra, Chandigarh, Dimapur, Jammu & Pune. 
AAI has already started work at most of these airports. 
GREENFIELD AIRPORTS:— New greenfield airports are c oming up at 
Hyderabad and Bangalore. In principle approval has been given for a 
greenfield airport at Mopa (Goa). Proposals for gre enfield airports at 
Durgapur (West Bengal), Navi Mumbai and Pune (Mahar ashtra), Pakyong 
(Sikkim), Cheithu (Kohima-Nagaland), Itanagar (Arunachal Pradesh) are under 
consideration. 
AAI have also taken up major Communications Navigation Surveillance (CNS) 
projects as part of modernization of airport infrastructure. 
(c) and (d) An Airport Development Cell is already functioning in the 
Airports Authority of India.

Opening of branches of UCBs  
†*302. MISS ANUSUIYA UIKEY: Will the Minister of FI NANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India contemplating giv ing permission to 
open more branches of banks to strengthen Urban Co-operative Banks; 
(b) the basis for considering any Urban Co-operative Bank as a weak bank; 
(c) the number of such branches of weak Urban Co-operative Banks in the 
country and the action being taken for improving their condition; and 
(d) by when the permission for opening new branches would be given? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (d) 
Yes, Sir, In the Mid-term Review of Annual Policy S tatement for the year 
2006-07, Reserve Bank of India has decided to allow  financially sound 
Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) registered in States  that have signed MoU 
with the Reserve Bank of India and those registered under the Multi-State Co-
operative Societies Act, 2002 to convert existing e xtention counters into full-
fledge branches subject to certain conditions menti oned in the guidelines 
issued on November 13, 2006. 
(b) and (c) Reserve Bank of the India has graded th ese banks in four 
categories Grade—I, Grade-ll Grade-Ill and Grade-IV  based on certain 
parameters Banks in Grade-Ill, and IV broadly corre spond to weak and sick 
category and have been graded as per the criterion given below:— 
Grade—III: 
(i) If CRAR falls below 75% of the minimum prescribed level, but 50% 
or above. 
(ii) Net NPA is 10% or more but less than 15% of ne t loans and 
advances, as on 31 March, or as identified by RBI, subsequently. 
(iii) Incurred net losses for two years out of last  three consecutive 
financial years after making adequate provision for  asset losses as 
indicated by the statutory auditors/RCS and/or RBI. 
Grade—IV: 
(i) If their CRAR is below 50% of the minimum prescribed level; and 
(ii) If net NPA is 15% or more of net loans and adv ances-as on 31 
March, or as identified by RBI, subsequently; or 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
(iii) If they show net losses (as per balance sheet ) for the last three 
consecutive financial years, ( i.e. the condition on CRAR together with 
any one of the two other conditions relating to Net NPA/net losses). 
To ensure regulatory coordination and cooperation u nder the existing legal 
framework, RBI has entered into MoU with nine State Governments. As part of 
the MOU, a Task Force for Urban Co-operative banks (TAFCUB) has been 
set up in each of the States which have signed the MoU tor identification and 
drawing up of a time bound action plan for revival of potentially viable 
UCBs and for non disruptive exit for nonviable UCBs. 
Based on TAFCUBs recommendations, supervisory actions that have been 
taxen include issue of license to unlicensed banks,  allowing merger of UCBs 
cancellation of license of unviable UCBs.etc. Furth er, certain other facilities 
like setting up of currency chest, selling mutal fu nds, providing foreign 
exchange services etc., have been extended to such banks in the MoU signed 
States.

financial institutes? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) 
As per information available with the Securities and Exchange Board of India 
(SEBI), the National value of Participatory Notes (PNs) has

increased from Rs. 1,17,325 crore in January 2006 t o Rs. 2,02,487 crore in

Investors (Flls) increased from Rs. 3,84,491 crore to Rs. 5,81,087 crore

Financial crunch at HCL  
*307. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HEA VY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the financial crunc h that the 
Hindustan Cables Limited in Andhra Pradesh is facing; 
(b) whether it is a fact that employees are also not be ing paid their salaries 
regularly; 
(c) whether the State Government of Andhra Pradesh has requested his 
Ministry to persuade Ministry of Communications and  Information 
Technology for some orders of cables, etc; 
6 

[20 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, what the Ministry has done in this regard; 
(e) whether NT, Kharagpur, proposed for taking up some diversification activities of 
HCL; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof and the reasons for the Ministry not approving the 
same? 
THE MINISTER OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC 
ENTERPRISES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) to (f) Hindustan Cable 
Limited (HCL), Kolkata is a Central Public Sector Enterprises and has been making 
losses since 1996. It has units at Rupnarainpur (West Bengal), Hyderabad (Andhra 
Pradesh) and Naini (Uttar Pradesh). The production operations in all the units are 
suspended for last three years due to, inter-alia, higher cost of production and steep 
fall in demand, because of which company is facing severe financial crunch. 
Consequently, HCL is not able to pay salary to its employees and has been dependent on 
budgetary support from Government for payment of salaries, Government has approved 
release of funds to HCL for payment of salary and wages to its employees upto 
December 2006. 
In response of the request to the Department of Telecommunication (DoT) made in 
September 2004 for placing orders on HCL, DoT expressed its inability to place additional 
orders, since HCL already had an outstanding order of 18.4 lakh conductor kilometer 
cable which it has not been able to deliver despite having received an advance of Rs. 239.78 
crore from Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. (BSNL). It has become difficult for HCL to 
manufacture the main line product namely Polythene Insulated Jelly Filled cables and 
Optical Fiber cables, as even the variable cost of production (cost of raw materials, 
power and freight) is higher than the price of cable offered by BSNL. 
HCL commissioned a tech no-economic study through NT Kharagpur which 
submitted its report in November 2004. The study pr oposed diversification in 
unrelated products and alternate products with an additional capital investment of Rs. 
194 crore in two phases over a period of 5-7 years for modernization and upgradation 
of equipments according to the diversification plan, over and above Draft Revival Scheme of 
Rs. 1448 crore submitted by M/s. SBI Caps, the Operating Agency appointed by BIFR. 
IIT Kharagpur in its report had mentioned the names of the alternative products like power 
cables. The IIT study Report was discussed in the meeting of Board for Revival of Public 
Sector Enterprises 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
(BRPSE) in September, 2006 and it was observed that  in the absence of any 
detailed feasibility study as to the demand of the product, the competition in 
the market place, the production capacities require d for breakeven levels and 
the capacity of HCL to compete, a decision on the p roposed strategy could 
not be taken. 
On the recommendations of BRPSE a fresh detailed te chno-economic 
feasibility study of HCL has been commissioned with  IIT Kharagpur on 
17.01.2007 which is to be completed in four months. 
Motors fuels under VAT   
*308. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of PE TROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact Government have received r epresentation from 
oil industry for bringing motor fuels under VAT as this will enable to 
reduce the burden of flaring crude prices on common man; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the VAT regime will enble to reationalise 
the varying State taxes; and 
(c) if so, by when it is expected to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI 
DEORA): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. As per Constitution, l evying of tax on sale or 
purchase (including VAT) of Motor Fuels comes withi n the purview of State 
Governments. An Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers (EC) has 
been constituted, inter-alia, to deliberate upon matters concerning Sales Tax 
and to make recommendations to the States in matter s concerning Sales 
Tax/VAT. Accordingly Petroleum Federation of India (Petrofed) on behalf of 
Oil Gas Industry had made a representation in July 2005 to the Chairman of 
Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers on V AT for giving the 
benefits of full set-off and credit mechanism avail able under VAT to the 
petroleum sector. As per the EC recommendations, pe trol, diesel, Aviation 
Turbine Fuel (ATF) and other motor spirits are subject to 20% floor rate of tax 
and have been kept outside VAT (i.e. non-vatable). The EC or the State 
Government have not taken any decision to bring motor spirits under VAT.

approval of their Board of Directors subject to Benchmark Prime Lending Rate (BPLR) 
and Spread guidelines. In order to enhance transparency in pricing of their loan 
products, banks have been advised by the RBI to fix their BPLR after taking into account 
(i) actual cost of funds, (ii) operating expenses and (iii) a minimum margin to cover 
regulatory requirement of provisioning/capital charge and profit margin and ensure 
that the BPLR truly reflects the actual cost. Individual banks, therefore, determine 
interest rates to be charged from a particular borrower subject to their BPLR and spread 
guidelines. However, loans up to Rs. 2 lakh carry the prescription of not exceeding the 
BPLR. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
RBI has also given freedom to commercial banks to f ix their own interest 
rates on domestic term deposits of various maturities with the prior approval of 
their respective Board of Directors with effect from October 22, 1997. As such, the 
rates of interest on deposits are being determined by the banks themselves. 
However, RBI regulates interest rates on savings bank accounts. 
As stated in the Third/Quarter Review of Annual Sta tement on Monetary 
Policy for 2006-07, issued on January 31, 2007, the Reserve Bank will ensure 
that appropriate liquidity is maintained in the sys tem so that all legitimate 
requirements of credit are met, particularly for pr oductive purposes, 
consistent with the objective of price and financial stability Towards this end, 
the Reserve Bank will continue its policy of active  demand management of 
liquidity through Open Market Operations (OMO) incl uding the Market 
Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), Liquidity Adjustment Fa cility (LAF) and Cash 
Reserve Rato (CRR).and using all the policy instruments at its disposal flexibly 
as and when the situation warrants.

Statement  
Details of New Initiatives Taken to Check Adulteration of Petrol/Diesel and 
Streamlining PDS Kerosene Distribution  
Checking adulteration is a continuous process and the Ministry of Petroleum & 
Natural Gas has been reviewing steps taken to curb adulteration from time to time. 
In the process, several technological and institutional measures have been taken to 
contain adulteration. The recent steps taken by the Ministry are summarized below: 
1 . Automation of Retail Outlets: In order to monitor the activities at retail outlets 
by adopting the latest technological improvements, automation of retail outlets is being 
implemented. MOP&NG has directed the oil marketing companies to complete 
automation of retail outlets selling more than 200 KL per month by March 2007 
2. Third Party Certification of Retail Outlets: OMCs have been directed to 
complete third party certification of all the retail outlets selling more than 100 KL per 
month by March 2007 
130 

[20 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
3. Monitoring of movement of Tank Trucks through Globa l Positioning 
System (GPS): In order to prevent adulteration during transportation, OMCs have 
been directed to install GPS for complete monitoring of the movement of all the 
company owned/dealer owned/ contractor owned tank trucks by March 2007. 
4. Marker System in Kerosene: To check adulteration in auto fuels, Government has 
asked public sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) to take various steps, including 
introduction of marker in adulterants. OMCs have commenced introduction of marker 
in kerosene on all India basis with effect from 1.10.2006. Under the new system, 
Marker is being put in kerosene in all depots. This system heralds the introduction of 
world class technology to curb and eventually eliminate the menace of adulteration of 
transportation fuels along the supply chain. With the marker's presence, adulteration 
even with very low levels of kerosene can be detected. MS/HSD Control Order, 2005, 
SKO Control Order, 1993 and MDG 2005 have been amended for making provision 
regarding introduction of marker system in Kerosene to check adulteration. A 
committee has been set up in the Ministry to monitor the progress of the marker 
system. Oil Marketing Companies in the Private Sector have also been simultaneously 
asked to introduce marker in Kerosene as is being done by Public Sector OMCs. 
5. Revising the Marketing Discipline Guidelines: The m arketing Discipline 
Guidelines (MDG) under which the oil marketing companies take penal actions against 
the erring dealers have been revised during August 2005 making the penal actions 
more stringent. As per MDG, 2005, a dealership would be terminated in the first instance 
of adulteration itself. 
6. Jan Kerosene Pariyojna: To streamline the PDS Kerosene distribution system 
and contain diversion of kerosene for adulteration and other unauthorized usages, Jan 
Kerosene Pariyojna (JKP) had been launched initially for a period of 6 months on a pilot 
basis in 414 blocks with effect from 2.10.2005. The Pilot scheme has been further 
extended upto 30.6.2007. 
7. Smart Card Scheme: With the objective of ensuring that the benefit of the 
subsidy reaches the targeted consumers in an efficient 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
and cost-effective manner and to prevent any leakages, this Ministry has proposed 
introduction of Smart Card System for distribution of PDS kerosene. The scheme is 
proposed to be introduced initially on an experimental basis. In the Pilot project, 
subsidized kerosene through Smart Card is proposed to be available to BPL families 
while all other ration card holders would be given non-subsidized kerosene. Oil Marketing 
Companies (OMCs) would ensure adequate availability of PDS as well as non-subsidized 
kerosene during the entire period of implementation of the Pilot.

Promotion of tourism through 'Incredible India' campaign  
†2389. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of TOURISM be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the total amount incurred by Government on the vigorous drive i.e. 'Incredible 
India' launched in the media and press these days; 
(b) the head-wise details of amount incurred out of this amount on the domestic 
as well as foreign communication mediums; 
(c) the details of amount incurred earlier on the similar publicity campaign of 
Atithi devo bhava', by Government; 
(d) the reasons for changing priorities on tourism by Government; and 
(e) the details of achievements made in promoting touri sm through such 
vigorous publicity campaigns? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) A sum of Rs. 
69.19 crore has already been incurred during the current financial year in respect of 
Incredible India centrialized media campaigns both in the domestic and overseas 
markets. 
(b) Asum of Rs. 15.70 crore and Rs. 53.49 crore have been incurred towards 
campaigns in the domestic and overseas markets respectively. 
(c) A total of Rs. 18.00 crore had been incurred on Atithi Devo Bhavah Publicity 
campaign undertaken in two phases in 2004-05 and 2005-06. 
(d) While priorities have not changed, the Government is putting greater emphasis on 
development of infrastructure at important tourist destinations/circuits and to 
promote and publicize various tourism products of India within the country and 
abroad. 
(e) There has been an increase of 45% during the last two years, in foreign tourist 
arrival to the country and the foreign exchange earnings during the same period have 
also increased by 62.2% in US dollar terms.

Conservation of rain water  
2402. MS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of WATER  
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) how much of rain water goes to the seas annually; 
(b) whether Government have any plan to conserve this water; 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
(c) if so, the details of the proposal; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAYPRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) The average annual 
precipitation is estimated as 4000 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) in the country. After 
accounting for the natural process of evaporation etc. the average annual water 
availability in the country is assessed as 1869 BCM. It is estimated that owing to 
topographic, hydrological and other constraints, the utilizable water is 1123 BCM. 
Rest of the water could be considered to be flowing down to sea. 
(b) and (c) Several measures for development and management of water resources 
are undertaken by the respective States Governments which include creation of 
storages, restoration of water bodies, rain water harvesting, artificial recharge to ground 
water and adoptbn of better management practices etc. State Governments conceive, 
plan and implement major, medium and minor schemes (both surface and ground water) 
for utilization of water resources. Storage capacity of about 213 BCM has been created 
so far. As per present assessment, the total estimated storage capacity of the various 
projects under construction is about 76 BCM. Further, the State Governments have 
identified various other schemes for investigation and planning and the estimated storage 
for such schemes is about 108 BCM. Government of India is providing central assistance 
to the State Governments through various schemes/ programmes, such as Accelerated 
Irrigation Benefits Programmes (AIBP); Command Area Development and Water 
Management (CADWM) Programme; National Project for Repair, Renovation and 
Restoration of Water Bodies directly linked to Agriculture etc. The Government of India 
also encourages rainwater harvesting and recharge to groundwater for conservation of 
water. 
(d) Does not arise.

Arsenic content in ground water  
     †2404. SHRI SATYAVARAT CHATURVEDI:                          
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per the report of scientists of the School of Studies 
in Chemestry of Pandit Ravi Shankar Shukla University, arsenic content in the 
ground water of Ambagarh Chauki, Korba, Kanker, Dhamtari, Bastar and Durg 
(Bhillai) of Chhattisgarh has been found above the danger mark; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that besides Chhattisgarh, arsenic content has also been 
found in excessive quantity in West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya 
Pradesh; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) what steps are being taken by Government to protect local people from the 
harmful effects of the arsenic content? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) As per information received from 
School of Studies in Chemistry, Pandit Ravi Shankar Shukla University, arsenic 
content in excess of maximum permissible limit of 0.05 mg/litre has been reported 
from Ambagarh Chauki and Kanker in Chhattisgarh. However, from Korba, Dhamtari, 
Bastar and Durg, no arsenic in ground water has been reported. Studies carried out by the 
Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) have also revealed presence of high arsenic 
content in some villages of Ambagarh Chauki block of Rajnandgaon district. 
(b) Besides Chhattisgarh, occurrence of high concentration of arsenic in ground 
water has been observed in West Bengal, in the depth zone of 20-80 m in the area 
east of river Bhagirathi in 79 blocks of 8 districts viz. Malda, Murshidabad, Nadia, North 
24 Parganas, South 24 Parganas, Hoogli, Howrah and Bardhaman In Bihar, parts of 12 
districts have been reported as arsenic affected. The reportedly affect districts are 
Bhojpur, Buxar, Vaishali, Saran, Samastipur, Begusarai, Patna, Khagaria, Munger, 
Bhagalpur, Katihar and Darbhanga. In Uttar Pradesh, Ballia and Gonda districts have 
been reported as arsenic 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
188 

[20 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
affected. There is no report of high arsenic content in ground water in Madhya 
Pradesh. 
(c) Arsenic contamination in ground water is caused due  to natural 
mechanism by which arsenic present in the water bea ring formations gets 
mobilized under reducing environment and is released into the ground water. 
(d) 'Water' being a State subject, necessary action to protect local . people 
from arsenic is to be taken by the respective States. However, various steps 
being taken by the Union Government and the States in this regard are given 
below:— 
West Bengal: 
(i) In order to delineate arsenic free deeper aquif ers, CGWB has 
undertaken ground water exploration in arsenic infe sted areas of West 
Bengal. Til! February, 2007,88 nos. of exploratory wells tapping different 
aquifers have been constructed in 32 blocks spreadi ng over 7 arsenic 
infested districts. The successful exploratory wells have been handed over 
to the user agencies for their water supply schemes. 
(ii) C3WB is also providing technical guidance for clearing of source for 
drinking water in arsenic affected areas in Source Finding Committee 
meeting for PHED, Government of West Bengal. 
(iii) Mass Awareness Programme and Water Management  Training 
Programme in different arsenic affected districts in West Bengal are being 
organized by CGWB to make aware the local people an d for providing 
technical guidance. 
(iv) To provide potable water to the people living in arsenic affected areas PHED, 
Government of West Bengal has taken up different Short Term, Medium 
Term and Long Term measures/schemes utilizing both groundwater and 
surface water. 
Bihar: 
(i) CGWB constructs heavy duty deep tube wells tapping arsenic free deeper 
aquifers up to 200 m depth below ground level and h andover these 
tubewells free of cost to the state PHED for immediate supply of arsenic 
free water. 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
(ii) CGWB is conducting awareness camps in the Arsenic affected areas. 
(iii) CGWB is conducting research to understand the origin and distribution of 
arsenic in ground water for adopting long term appr opriate remedial 
measures. 
Steps being taken by PHED, Government of Bihar: 
(i) Testing of water samples and marking the affected structures as unsafe for 
drinking use. 
(ii) Awareness Camps being organized for the masses in the affected areas. 
(iii) Sanitary wells are being constructed in each of the affected village. 
(iv) Construction of deep bore wells (upto 125m depth) fitted with hand pumps to tap 
the Arsenic free deeper aquifer. 
(v) Multi village water supply scheme covering 39 villages of Barhara block of 
Bhojpur district. 
(vi) Roof top rain water harvesting being promoted in the affected villages. 
Uttar Pradesh: 
CGWB is taking up exploratory drilling in arsenic infested area of Uttar Pradesh 
by deployment of its four drilling rigs identifying suitable aquifer. The exploratory 
wells tapping the deeper aquifer encountered in the above districts in the depth range of 
180—435m. below ground level having arsenic concentration within permissible 
limit are to be handed over to U.P. Jal Nigam for their utilization. 
In addition, the Union Ministry of Rural Development (Department of Drinking 
Water Supply) under the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission provides 
financial and technical assistance to States through a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, 
namely Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) for provision of safe 
drinking water to the rural population as per the stipulated norms. In order to provide 
focused attention to tackle water quality problems, Sub-Mission guidelines under ARWSP 
have been revised in February, 2006, wherein, 20% of ARWSP funds is retained at the 
Centre and released to States on need-basis.

  2407.    SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: 
SHRI KAMALAKHTAR: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India does not have adequ ate infrastructure to 
capture the rainwater and the country has been sitt ing over new project for 
too long-so long that they become unaffordable; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that it takes a good mons oon to highlight the 
need for better storage and conservation of rainwater; and 
(c) if so, what steps Government propose to take to pla n for better storage 
and conservation of rainwater to pull India out of an alarming water crisis in 
the years to Come? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) The 
average annual rainfall of the country is about 1170 mm. However, there is very 
high temporal and spatial variation in rainfall. Wi th a view to conserve water, 
several water resources development projects have been taken up in the country. 
There has been considerable progress in respect of water resources development 
in India since independence through major, medium a nd minor irrigation 
schemes and multipurpose projects. The live storage capacity of the completed 
dam projects is estimated to be 213 Billion Cubic M etre (BCM) which was 
only about 15.6 BCM at the time of independence. Be sides, as per present 
assessment, the total estimated storage capacity of  the various projects under 
construction is about 76 BCM. Further, the State Go vernments have 
identified various other schemes for investigation and planning and the 
estimated storage for such schemes is about 108 BCM. 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2007] 
Measures for development and management of water resources are undertaken by the 
respective State Governments which include creation of storage through major, medium and 
minor irrigation projects, restoration of water bodies, rain water harvesting, artificial recharge 
to ground water and adoption of better management practices etc. Government of India 
provides assistance to the State Governments through various schemes/ programmes, such 
as Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP); Command Area Development and 
Water Management (CADWM) Programme; National Project for Repair, Renovation 
and Restoration of Water Bodies directly linked to Agriculture etc. The Government of 
India also encourages rainwater harvesting and rech arge to groundwater for 
conservation of water.

Ministry of Water Resources (MOWR) (erstwhile Minis try of Irrigation) and 
Central Water Commission (CWC) formulated a National Perspective Plan (NPP) 
for Water Resources Development in 1980 envisaging inter-basin transfer of 
water from surplus basins to deficit basins/areas f or optimum utilization of 
water resources. The NPP comprises two components, namely, Himalayan 
Rivers Development Component and Peninsular Rivers Development. 
National Water Development Agency (NWDA) was set up under the MOWR

generation, domestic & industrial water supply bene fits to the STate of Bihar.
